report:
Based on strong and consistent evidence across large observational studies, randomized trials, and meta-analyses, the claim is well supported.

**Conclusion: True.** Bystander hands-only (chest-compression-only) CPR is associated with significantly greater survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) compared with no bystander CPR at all.

**Evidence:**
- The American Heart Association's science advisory concluded that adult OHCA victims receiving bystander hands-only CPR have similar—and clearly better—survival than those receiving no bystander CPR, while performing similarly to conventional CPR with rescue breaths (https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/circulationaha.107.189380).
- A meta-analysis in *Circulation* found that dispatcher-assisted compression-only CPR was associated with improved survival compared with standard CPR, and both forms of bystander CPR vastly outperformed no CPR (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2987687/).
- Large registry-based studies (e.g., the multinational cohort analysis) show that after multivariable adjustment, both compression-only and conventional bystander CPR were associated with substantially higher survival compared to no bystander CPR (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9803815/).
- Additional cohort data from Japan and other national registries confirm bystander CPR (chest-compression-only) roughly doubles survival and neurological recovery odds versus no bystander intervention, reinforcing the biological plausibility that early perfusion via chest compressions is the critical determinant of outcome, more so than ventilation, in most adult witnessed arrests (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9803815/).

**Caveats:** The survival benefit is most robust for adult, witnessed, cardiac-cause arrests. For pediatric and asphyxia-related arrests, conventional CPR (with rescue breaths) may confer additional benefit over compressions alone, though both still outperform no CPR.

**Bottom line:** The claim is accurate — hands-only bystander CPR meaningfully improves survival relative to no bystander CPR in adult OHCA, which is why it is endorsed by the AHA for lay rescuers.
